q: Non-sterilization surgeries in the shelter, including dentistry, must adhere to:
o: Relaxed biosecurity, given the high bacterial load of shelter populations
The ASV spay-neuter guidelines for surgical suite, anesthesia, analgesia and sterility
No particular standard if done in the medical wing
e: All shelter surgery, including dentistry, must meet the ASV spay-neuter standards for suite, anesthesia, analgesia and aseptic technique.

q: Why is non-anesthetic dental probing, scaling and polishing considered unacceptable?
o: It alters the oral microbiome and spreads infection between species
Significant disease can be missed and the restraint causes severe stress and risk of serious injury from sharp instruments or bites
It needs intraoral radiographs that only work on awake patients
It breaches commercial dishwasher sanitation standards
e: Without sedation, pathology is missed and the patient and staff are placed at real risk; sedation is required.

q: A hoarding-case cat has a painful mouth but the shelter has no intraoral radiography. The correct approach is:
o: Defer all dental care until imaging is acquired
Treat the painful mouth even without radiology, because dental disease has serious welfare implications
Give long-term steroids and avoid surgery to reduce length of stay
e: Welfare comes first; a painful mouth is treated even when advanced imaging is unavailable.

q: The overarching goal of balanced anesthesia, optimal perioperative care and low-stress handling is to ensure:
o: Lower disinfectant costs in the surgical suite
Not only survival but the long-term health and vitality of the patient
Elimination of the preoperative physical exam
e: The aim is durable health and vitality, so the animal enters adoption resilient, not merely survival of the procedure.

q: Before GA or surgery, the correct examination sequence is:
o: The technician's assessment alone is sufficient; the vet reviews logs afterward
A trained technician performs the initial vital-parameter assessment, then the veterinarian performs a complete PE before any drugs are given
The vet may skip the PE when a signed intake form exists
The exam is deferred to the recovery period
e: A tiered approach is used, but a veterinary PE must precede administration of any GA or analgesic agent.

q: A cat has moderate anemia, about 6% dehydration and an asymptomatic low-grade heart murmur. The ASA class is:
e: Moderate systemic disturbance with clinical signs the animal cannot fully compensate for is ASA III.

q: A dog has severe uremia, acute renal failure, clinical pulmonary disease and recent trauma but is not moribund. The ASA class is:
e: Significant illness with significant compromise (uremia, renal failure, clinical pulmonary disease, trauma) is ASA IV; ASA V is reserved for moribund or comatose animals.

q: Regarding routine preoperative blood work, the best stance is:
o: It changes the surgical technique in more than half of shelter cases
Age should not be the sole determinant; in the cited data the anesthetic protocol changed in only 0.2% of dogs, so health status and disease potential drive testing
The ASV mandates it for every animal over 5 years of age
Point-of-care testing is useless and should be replaced by full electrolyte panels
e: Routine screening rarely alters management in healthy animals; clinical status, not age, guides whether to test.

q: Which presentation is an explicit reason to defer elective sterilization?
o: Known or suspected intestinal or urinary obstruction
e: Obstructive disease is a serious problem that defers elective surgery; the other items do not.

q: Which must a standardized intake form capture before GA or surgery?
o: Current or recent medications (including parasiticides) and satisfaction of post-operative fasting requirements
The transport route to the shelter
e: Medication history and fasting status are essential to avoid drug interactions and aspiration risk.

q: A feral cat is lunging in the trap. How does the preoperative PE requirement apply?
o: Pin the cat without sedation to auscultate the thorax
A volunteer performs a full unsedated PE first
A preoperative PE is required before GA except when the animal is fearful, aggressive or feral
e: The PE-before-GA rule has an explicit exception for fearful, aggressive or feral animals, where an unsedated exam is unsafe.

q: Chamber induction with inhalant gas should be avoided at all costs because it:
o: Causes severe waste-gas accumulation, prolonged sympathomimetic windup and lethal high inhalant concentrations
Drops intraocular pressure and invalidates ophthalmic screening
Degrades plastic or glass containment tanks
e: Chambers produce dangerous gas accumulation, excessive sympathetic windup and the risk of lethal inhalant concentrations.

q: A direct drawback of mask induction is that it:
o: Is non-sympathomimetic and drops heart rate
Causes unnecessary stress, uncontrolled loss of consciousness, gas waste, and bronchoirritation with risk of gastric aspiration via an unprotected airway
Takes at least 45 minutes to reach a surgical plane
Is only compatible with ASA V patients
e: Masking forces the animal through an agitated phase, wastes gas, and leaves the airway unprotected against aspiration.

q: If mask maintenance is being required too often, an appropriate corrective strategy is to:
o: Increase the inhalant concentration to speed up surgery
Switch the whole population to chamber induction
Use a protocol that requires intubation rather than masking, or one with better analgesics and sedatives
e: Frequent masking signals an unstable protocol; move to intubation or improve the injectable sedation and analgesia.

q: Which dogs should be prioritized for endotracheal intubation?
o: Lean athletic dogs with confirmed 12-hour fasts
Most unfasted dogs or those with unknown fasting status, overweight dogs, and brachycephalic dogs
Puppies under 6 weeks for suture removal
Dogs with normal airways and low vagal tone
e: Aspiration and airway-occlusion risk is highest in unfasted, overweight and brachycephalic dogs, so intubation is prioritized.

q: An explicit drawback of endotracheal intubation listed in your notes is:
o: Regurgitation or vomiting, increased intracranial and ocular pressure, and increased vagal tone
Breakdown of epoxy flooring in the suite
e: Laryngeal stimulation can trigger vagal responses, raise intracranial and ocular pressure, and provoke regurgitation.

q: A capnograph shows a low end-tidal CO2 (ETCO2). A primary cause is:
o: Build-up of CO2 within the anesthetic machine
Hyperventilation, low perfusion states or hypothermia
e: Low ETCO2 reflects either rapid clearance (hyperventilation) or reduced delivery of CO2 to the lungs (low perfusion, hypothermia).

q: A high ETCO2 reading indicates:
o: Severe hyperventilation from deep CNS depression
Hypoventilation, excessive metabolism or heat, or build-up of CO2 within the machine
High perfusion combined with extreme hypothermia
e: High ETCO2 points to CO2 retention from hypoventilation, increased production, or spent absorbent in the circuit.

q: The risk of relying on a single monitoring variable is that it:
o: Can lead to an inadequate plane of anesthesia, or to excessive depth with risk of emergencies
Removes the need for chest auscultation
Forces the patient into ASA IV status
e: No single parameter is reliable alone; multi-parameter monitoring prevents an undetected depth crisis.

q: The primary benefit of anesthetic monitoring is that it:
o: Enhances recognition of worrisome trends and provides a legal record of significant events
Converts ASA status into an epidemic curve
e: Monitoring catches dangerous trends early and documents significant events for the medical and legal record.

q: Per RECOVER 2024, the correct epinephrine dose during CPR is:
o: 0.01 mg/kg IV or IO every 3–5 minutes
e: RECOVER 2024: epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg IV or IO, repeated every 3–5 minutes (approximately every other CPR cycle). The ET dose is 0.1 mg/kg.

q: An anesthetized dog's MAP drops to 52 mmHg. The first intervention is:
o: Start dopamine CRI at 10 mcg/kg/min immediately
Increase the isoflurane to stabilize the plane
Reduce inhalant concentration and give an isotonic crystalloid bolus (5–10 mL/kg)
e: The treatment ladder starts with reducing inhalant (vasodilation is dose-dependent) and a fluid bolus. Vasopressors come after fluids fail.

q: For ventricular fibrillation in a dog unresponsive to CPR, the preferred anti-arrhythmic per RECOVER is:
e: RECOVER recommends amiodarone as first-line for VF/pulseless VT. Lidocaine is an alternative in dogs but not preferred. Lidocaine is not recommended at this dose in cats.

q: Per RECOVER 2024, the correct compression rate during CPR is:
e: RECOVER 2024: 100–120 compressions per minute, compressing 1/3 to 1/2 of the chest width. Rotate compressor every 2 minutes.

q: An anesthetized cat has apnea for 40 seconds. The correct immediate action is:
o: Begin manual IPPV at 10–15 mL/kg tidal volume, 8–12 breaths/min
e: Apnea over 30 seconds requires immediate manual ventilation. Reduce inhalant and check tube position simultaneously.

q: Biphasic external defibrillation energy in dogs and cats per RECOVER 2024 is:
e: Biphasic external defibrillation is 2–4 J/kg; monophasic requires more (4–6 J/kg). Always start at the lower end.

q: Why is lidocaine used with caution in cats during CPR?
o: Cats are sensitive to lidocaine toxicity; the 2 mg/kg anti-arrhythmic dose used in dogs is not recommended in cats
Lidocaine is not a RECOVER-approved drug
Lidocaine prolongs the QT interval only in cats
e: Cats are more sensitive to lidocaine toxicity; amiodarone is the preferred anti-arrhythmic in both species.

q: The CMPS-SF (Glasgow Composite Measure Pain Scale Short Form) intervention threshold for dogs is:
e: CMPS-SF intervention threshold is 6/20. At this score or above, rescue analgesia is indicated for dogs.

q: Which validated pain scale is designed and validated specifically for cats?
e: UNESP-Botucatu was validated for acute post-operative feline pain (threshold 8/27). CMPS-SF is validated for dogs.

q: A cat's UNESP-Botucatu pain score is 9/27 post-OHE. The intervention threshold is 8. The correct action is:
o: Remove the E-collar to reduce stress
e: 9/27 exceeds the 8/27 intervention threshold; rescue analgesia is indicated immediately.

q: Which pain scale is most recommended for shelter settings due to ease of staff training?
e: The CSU scale trains quickly and is widely used in shelter and high-volume settings, though CMPS-SF and UNESP-Botucatu provide the validated thresholds for ABVP exam purposes.

q: Standard activity restriction after routine soft-tissue surgery is:
o: Leash walks only; no running, jumping, rough play, or swimming for 10–14 days
No restriction for cats; dogs restricted 3 days
e: Standard restriction is 10–14 days of limited activity to allow incision healing.

q: When should the E-collar be applied after surgery?
o: After the animal is ambulatory and aware
Only if the animal tries to lick
Before full recovery from anesthesia, while still in the immediate post-op period
e: E-collar must be on before the animal is fully awake; a recovering animal can traumatize a fresh incision in seconds.

q: Which post-surgical finding requires immediate attention?
o: Dehiscence — any gap in the suture line
Small amount of clear serous fluid in the first hour
e: Dehiscence requires immediate attention due to risk of contamination, herniation, and serious complications.

q: In a surgical patient being assessed for discharge, which finding should prompt continued monitoring rather than release?
o: Has eaten a full meal immediately after anesthesia
e: Eating immediately post-anesthesia is not a discharge criterion and risks vomiting. The other three are standard criteria.

q: Which chronic medication should be withheld on the morning of anesthesia?
o: An ACE inhibitor such as enalapril or benazepril
e: ACE inhibitors are discontinued the day of anesthesia because inhalant vasodilation plus ACE blockade can cause hypotension refractory to fluids and pressors. Thyroid, cardiac (pimobendan/furosemide) and antibiotic meds are continued.

q: A herding-breed dog carries the MDR1 (ABCB1) mutation. Anesthetic adjustment is to:
o: Increase all drug doses for faster effect
Reduce acepromazine and potentially butorphanol doses
e: MDR1/ABCB1 mutation alters CNS drug handling; reduce acepromazine and potentially butorphanol. The mutation is classic in Collies and Australian Shepherds.

q: The induction agent of choice for a patient with significant cardiovascular disease is:
e: Etomidate has minimal cardiovascular effects, making it ideal for cardiac patients; the trade-off is myoclonus, pain on injection, and adrenocortical suppression. Co-induce with a benzodiazepine.

q: Preoxygenation with 100% O2 for ~3 minutes before induction provides approximately:
o: 6 minutes of adequate hemoglobin saturation during apnea
e: About 3 minutes of preoxygenation buys ~6 minutes of adequate saturation during apnea/intubation — critical in airway disease, difficult intubation, and pregnancy.

q: For a feline castration testicular block, many clinicians prefer lidocaine over bupivacaine because:
o: Lidocaine has a higher safety margin if accidentally injected IV into the vascular testis
Bupivacaine is not effective in cats
e: The testes are highly vascular; lidocaine's wider safety margin on inadvertent IV injection makes it the pragmatic choice despite its shorter duration.

q: AAHA's headline recommendation for surgical analgesia is to:
o: Rely on a single full mu opioid
Use local anesthetics, insofar as possible, with every surgical procedure
Reserve analgesia until pain is observed
e: AAHA stresses multimodal, pre-emptive analgesia and specifically recommends using local anesthetics with every surgical procedure; local blocks completely interrupt pain transmission and lower inhalant needs.

q: An anesthetized dog is hypotensive from inhalant-induced vasodilation with good contractility. The most rational support drug is:
e: Match the drug to the cause: vasodilation calls for a vasoconstrictor (phenylephrine/norepinephrine). Inotropes (dopamine/dobutamine) are for poor contractility; ephedrine does both.

q: A surgical plane of anesthesia is best indicated by:
o: A brisk palpebral reflex and strong jaw tone
Absent palpebral reflex, mild jaw tone, a central-to-ventromedial eye position, and no purposeful movement
e: Surgical depth: absent palpebral reflex, mild jaw tone, ventromedial eye position, no purposeful movement — combined with electronic monitoring, not either alone.

q: Regarding the timing of anesthetic deaths, AAHA reports that most occur:
o: In the postoperative period, most within the first 3 hours
e: Roughly 47–60% of anesthetic deaths occur postoperatively, most within the first 3 hours — so recovery monitoring must be as vigilant as maintenance.
